claim: The hippocampus maps spatial and temporal distances between events encountered along a route through a virtual city.
source: We previously demonstrated that the hippocampus maps spatial and temporal distances between events encountered along a route through a virtual city (Deuker et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Deuker et al., 2016

claim: Multi-voxel representations in the anterior-lateral entorhinal cortex (alEC) specifically reflect the temporal event structure after learning.
source: Here, we demonstrate that multi-voxel representations in the anterior-lateral entorhinal cortex (alEC) — the human homologue of the rodent lateral entorhinal cortex — specifically reflect the temporal event structure after learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The alEC is the human homologue of the rodent lateral entorhinal cortex.
source: the anterior-lateral entorhinal cortex (alEC) — the human homologue of the rodent lateral entorhinal cortex
evidence: This is established knowledge cited elsewhere in the manuscript (Navarro Schröder et al., 2015; Maass et al., 2015)

claim: Holistic representations of the sequence structure related to memory recall.
source: Holistic representations of the sequence structure related to memory recall and the timeline of events could be reconstructed from entorhinal multi-voxel patterns.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing correlation with recall behavior

claim: The timeline of events could be reconstructed from entorhinal multi-voxel patterns.
source: Holistic representations of the sequence structure related to memory recall and the timeline of events could be reconstructed from entorhinal multi-voxel patterns.
evidence: Supported by multidimensional scaling analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: The lateral entorhinal cortex of navigating rodents carries temporal information in population signals.
source: dovetailing with temporal information carried by population signals in the lateral entorhinal cortex of navigating rodents
evidence: Supported by citation to rodent electrophysiology studies (Tsao et al., 2018)

claim: The alEC activates during temporal memory retrieval.
source: alEC activations during temporal memory retrieval
evidence: Supported by citation to Montchal et al., 2019

claim: Space and time constitute fundamental dimensions along which our experience is organized.
source: Space and time have been suggested to constitute fundamental dimensions along which our experience is organized (Konkel and Cohen, 2009; Ekstrom and Ranganath, 2018; Bellmund et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical frameworks

claim: The hippocampus is a core structure for episodic memory.
source: the hippocampus — a core structure for episodic memory (Scoville and Milner, 1957; Squire, 1982)
evidence: Established knowledge supported by classic citations

claim: The hippocampus codes locations in space.
source: the role of the hippocampus — a core structure for episodic memory (Scoville and Milner, 1957; Squire, 1982) — in coding locations in space (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Moser et al., 2017; Epstein et al., 2017)

claim: The hippocampus codes moments in time.
source: the role of the hippocampus — a core structure for episodic memory (Scoville and Milner, 1957; Squire, 1982) — in coding locations in space (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Moser et al., 2017; Epstein et al., 2017) and moments in time (Pastalkova et al., 2008; MacDonald et al., 2011; Eichenbaum, 2014; Ranganath, 2019; Howard, 2018) is well-established.

claim: The hippocampus forms integrated maps reflecting the temporal and spatial structure of event memories.
source: The similarity patterns of mnemonic representations suggest that the hippocampus forms integrated maps reflecting the temporal and spatial structure of event memories (Deuker et al., 2016; Nielson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Activity in the hippocampal-entorhinal region is sensitive to Euclidean distances during navigation.
source: Consistently, activity in the hippocampal-entorhinal region has been demonstrated to be sensitive to Euclidean distances as well as the lengths of shortest paths to goals during navigation (Spiers and Maguire, 2007; Viard et al., 2011; Sherrill et al., 2013; Howard et al., 2014; Chrastil et al., 2015; Spiers and Barry, 2015).

claim: Activity in the hippocampal-entorhinal region is sensitive to the lengths of shortest paths to goals during navigation.
source: Consistently, activity in the hippocampal-entorhinal region has been demonstrated to be sensitive to Euclidean distances as well as the lengths of shortest paths to goals during navigation (Spiers and Maguire, 2007; Viard et al., 2011; Sherrill et al., 2013; Howard et al., 2014; Chrastil et al., 2015; Spiers and Barry, 2015).

claim: The lateral entorhinal cortex is strongly connected to the hippocampus.
source: Evidence suggests that neural ensembles in the lateral entorhinal cortex (EC), which is strongly connected to the hippocampus (Witter et al., 2017), carry temporal information in freely moving rodents (Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to anatomical connectivity study

claim: Neural ensembles in the lateral entorhinal cortex carry temporal information in freely moving rodents.
source: Evidence suggests that neural ensembles in the lateral entorhinal cortex (EC), which is strongly connected to the hippocampus (Witter et al., 2017), carry temporal information in freely moving rodents (Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2018

claim: Temporal information could be decoded from lateral EC population activity with high accuracy.
source: Specifically, temporal information could be decoded from population activity with high accuracy (Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2018

claim: Temporal information in the lateral EC arises from the integration of experience rather than an explicit clocking signal.
source: This temporal information was suggested to arise from the integration of experience rather than an explicit clocking signal (Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2018

claim: The human anterior-lateral entorhinal cortex is the homologue region of the rodent lateral entorhinal cortex.
source: Recently, the human anterior-lateral entorhinal cortex (alEC), the homologue region of the rodent lateral entorhinal cortex (Navarro Schröder et al., 2015; Maass et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Navarro Schröder et al., 2015 and Maass et al., 2015

claim: The alEC, perirhinal cortex, and a network of brain regions including the hippocampus, medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex and angular gyrus have been implicated in the recall of temporal information.
source: Recently, the human anterior-lateral entorhinal cortex (alEC), the homologue region of the rodent lateral entorhinal cortex (Navarro Schröder et al., 2015; Maass et al., 2015), as well as the perirhinal cortex and a network of brain regions including the hippocampus, the medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex and angular gyrus have been implicated in the recall of temporal information (Montchal et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Montchal et al., 2019

claim: These regions responded more strongly for high compared to low accuracy retrieval of temporal information.
source: These regions responded more strongly for high compared to low accuracy retrieval of when in time snapshots from a sitcom appeared over the course of the episode viewed in the experiment (Montchal et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Montchal et al., 2019

claim: Participants can successfully recall spatial and temporal relations of events defined by object encounters in a virtual city.
source: Using this paradigm and data, we previously demonstrated that participants can successfully recall spatial and temporal relations of events defined by object encounters in a virtual city and that the change of hippocampal representations reflects an integrated event map of the remembered distance structure (Deuker et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deuker et al., 2016

claim: The change of hippocampal representations reflects an integrated event map of the remembered distance structure.
source: Using this paradigm and data, we previously demonstrated that participants can successfully recall spatial and temporal relations of events defined by object encounters in a virtual city and that the change of hippocampal representations reflects an integrated event map of the remembered distance structure (Deuker et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deuker et al., 2016

claim: The change of multi-voxel pattern similarity through learning in the alEC specifically reflects the temporal structure of the event sequence.
source: Here, we show that the change of multi-voxel pattern similarity through learning in the alEC specifically reflects the temporal structure of the event sequence.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data

claim: Participants navigated repeated laps of a route along which they encountered chests containing different objects.
source: Participants navigated repeated laps of a route along which they encountered chests containing different objects (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Describes the experimental procedure with reference to figures

claim: Object images were presented twelve times in the picture viewing tasks before and after learning, using the same random order in both scanning runs.
source: Specifically, we presented object images twelve times in the picture viewing tasks before and after learning, using the same random order in both scanning runs.

claim: Temporal and spatial object relationships were dissociated through the use of teleporters along the route.
source: Importantly, we dissociated temporal from Euclidean and geodesic spatial object relationships through the use of teleporters along the route (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Describes the experimental design with reference to figure

claim: The change in multi-voxel pattern similarity in alEC between pre- and post-learning scans was negatively correlated with the sequence structure.
source: The change in multi-voxel pattern similarity in alEC between pre- and post-learning scans was negatively correlated with the sequence structure (Figure 2A and Figure 2B, T(25)=- 3.75, p=0.001, alpha-level of 0.0125, Bonferroni-corrected for four comparisons)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: After relative to before learning, objects encountered in temporal proximity were represented more similarly compared to object pairs further separated in time.
source: After relative to before learning, objects encountered in temporal proximity were represented more similarly compared to object pairs further separated in time (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Pattern similarity change was negatively correlated with temporal distances after excluding comparisons of objects encountered in direct succession from the analysis.
source: Pattern similarity change was negatively correlated with temporal distances after excluding comparisons of objects encountered in direct succession from the analysis (T(25)=-2.00, p=0.029, one-sided test, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The observed effect speaks for holistic representations of temporal structure in the alEC.
source: speaking for holistic representations of temporal structure in the alEC and ruling out that the effect we observed is largely driven by increased similarity of temporally adjacent objects.
evidence: Inference based on the analysis excluding adjacent objects

claim: Participants with stronger correlations between alEC pattern similarity change and the temporal task structure tended to recall objects together that were encountered in temporal proximity along the route.
source: Specifically, participants with stronger correlations between alEC pattern similarity change and the temporal task structure tended to recall objects together that were encountered in temporal proximity along the route (Pearson r = −0.53, p=0.006, CIs: −0.76,–0.19, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of experimental data

claim: Pattern similarity change in alEC was not correlated significantly with Euclidean spatial distances.
source: Pattern similarity change in alEC did not correlate significantly with Euclidean spatial distances (T(25)=0.81, p=0.420)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Pattern similarity change in pmEC did not correlate with Euclidean distances.
source: pattern similarity change in posterior-medial EC (pmEC) did not correlate with Euclidean (T(25)=0.58, p=0.583)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Pattern similarity change in pmEC did not correlate with temporal distances.
source: pattern similarity change in posterior-medial EC (pmEC) did not correlate with Euclidean (T(25)=0.58, p=0.583) or temporal (T(25)=1.73, p=0.089) distances.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Temporal distances between objects during the first picture viewing task were not related to alEC pattern similarity change.
source: Temporal distances between objects during the first picture viewing task were not related to alEC pattern similarity change (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; T(24)=-0.29 p=0.776, one outlier excluded, see Materials and methods)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Correlations with elapsed time between objects during navigation were significantly more negative than correlations with temporal distances during the first picture viewing task.
source: and correlations with elapsed time between objects during navigation were significantly more negative (T(24)=-1.76 p=0.045; one-sided test)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The timeline of events can be reconstructed from pattern similarity change in alEC.
source: Can we reconstruct the timeline of events from pattern similarity change in alEC?

claim: The reconstructed temporal coordinates mirrored the time points at which objects were encountered during the task.
source: The reconstructed temporal coordinates, transformed into the original value range using Procrustes analysis (Figure 3A), mirrored the time points at which objects were encountered during the task (Figure 3B, Pearson correlation between reconstructed and true time points, r = 0.56, p=0.023, bootstrapped 95% confidence interval: 0.21, 0.79).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of reconstruction shown in Figure 3

claim: The Procrustes distance from fitting to the true timeline was smaller than the 5th percentile of the surrogate distribution.
source: The Procrustes distance from fitting to the true timeline was smaller than the 5th percentile of the surrogate distribution generated via 10000 random shuffles (Figure 3D, p=0.026).
evidence: Supported by permutation testing shown in Figure 3D

claim: A significant interaction was observed between EC subregion and distance type.
source: Crucially, we observed a significant interaction between EC subregion and distance type (F(1,25)=7.40, p=0.011, Figure 2B and E).

claim: The main effect of EC subregion was significant.
source: Further, the main effect of EC subregion was significant (F(1,25)=5.18, p=0.029)

claim: The main effect of distance type was not significant.
source: while the main effect of distance type was not (F(1,25)=0.84, p=0.367).

claim: There were significant differences between the mapping of temporal and spatial distances in alEC.
source: Based on the significant interaction, we conducted planned post-hoc comparisons, which revealed significant differences (Bonferroni-corrected alpha-level of 0.025) between the mapping of temporal and spatial distances in alEC (T(25)=-2.91, p=0.007)

claim: There was a significant difference between temporal mapping in alEC compared to pmEC.
source: and a significant difference between temporal mapping in alEC compared to pmEC (T(25)=-3.52, p=0.001).

claim: Pattern similarity change in alEC correlated significantly with ordinal temporal distances.
source: Pattern similarity change in alEC correlated significantly with ordinal temporal distances (Figure 4, T(25)=-3.37, p=0.002)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: Entorhinal pattern similarity change was not correlated with geodesic distances based on shortest paths between locations using all positions not obstructed by buildings or other obstacles.
source: Entorhinal pattern similarity change was not correlated with geodesic distances based on shortest paths between locations using all positions not obstructed by buildings or other obstacles (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, alEC: T(25)=0.82, p=0.436, pmEC: T(25)=0.73, p=0.479)

claim: Entorhinal pattern similarity change was not correlated with geodesic distances based on shortest paths using only the street network.
source: or based on shortest paths using only the street network (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, alEC: T(25)=0.36, p=0.715, pmEC: T(25)=0.92, p=0.375).

claim: Spatial and temporal signal-to-noise ratios did not differ between alEC and pmEC.
source: Spatial and temporal signal-to-noise ratios did not differ between alEC and pmEC (Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Supported by signal-to-noise analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: Classifier accuracies exceeded chance levels in the lateral occipital cortex.
source: We observed classifier accuracies exceeding chance levels in the lateral occipital cortex (LOC, Figure 2—figure supplement 4, T(25)=7.54, p<0.001, see Materials and methods)

claim: The lateral occipital cortex is involved in visual object processing.
source: We observed classifier accuracies exceeding chance levels in the lateral occipital cortex (LOC, Figure 2—figure supplement 4, T(25)=7.54, p<0.001, see Materials and methods) — known to be involved in visual object processing (Grill-Spector et al., 2001).

claim: In the entorhinal cortex, classification accuracies did not exceed chance levels.
source: In the entorhinal cortex, classification accuracies did not exceed chance levels (alEC: T(25)=-0.08, p=0.941; pmEC: T(25)=0.53, p=0.621).

claim: In the entorhinal cortex, classifier evidence did not exceed chance levels for the three objects preceding an object.
source: In the entorhinal cortex, classifier evidence did not exceed chance levels for the three objects preceding (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, alEC: most extreme T(25)=1.13; minimum p=0.270; pmEC: most extreme T(25)=1.00; min. p=0.332)
evidence: Supported by lag analysis of classifier predictions

claim: In the entorhinal cortex, classifier evidence did not exceed chance levels for the three objects following an object.
source: or following (alEC: most extreme T(25)=-2.07; min. p=0.055; pmEC: most extreme T(25)=-0.83; min. p=0.414) an object.
evidence: Supported by lag analysis of classifier predictions

claim: Within the EC, only representations in the anterior-lateral subregion changed to resemble the temporal structure of the event sequence.
source: Collectively, our findings demonstrate that, within the EC, only representations in the anterior-lateral subregion changed to resemble the temporal structure of the event sequence and that this mapping was specific to the temporal rather than the spatial dimension.

claim: The temporal mapping in alEC was specific to the temporal rather than the spatial dimension.
source: Collectively, our findings demonstrate that, within the EC, only representations in the anterior-lateral subregion changed to resemble the temporal structure of the event sequence and that this mapping was specific to the temporal rather than the spatial dimension.

claim: alEC representations reflect the experienced temporal event structure.
source: We examined the similarity of multi-voxel patterns to demonstrate that alEC representations reflect the experienced temporal event structure.

claim: These representations related to a holistic temporal map of the sequence structure despite being cued in random order after learning.
source: Despite being cued in random order after learning, these representations related to a holistic temporal map of the sequence structure.
evidence: Inference from experimental design and results

claim: Entorhinal pattern similarity change correlated with participants' recall behavior.
source: Moreover, entorhinal pattern similarity change correlated with participants' recall behavior and we recovered the timeline of events during learning from these representations.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: The timeline of events during learning was recovered from alEC representations.
source: Moreover, entorhinal pattern similarity change correlated with participants' recall behavior and we recovered the timeline of events during learning from these representations.
evidence: Supported by multidimensional scaling analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: Time could be decoded with higher accuracies from the lateral EC than the medial EC and hippocampal subfield CA3.
source: Time could be decoded with higher accuracies from the lateral EC than the medial EC and hippocampal subfield CA3.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2018

claim: During a structured task in which the animal ran repeated laps on a maze, neural trajectories through population activity space were similar across trials.
source: During a structured task in which the animal ran repeated laps on a maze separated into different trials, neural trajectories through population activity space were similar across trials, illustrating that the dynamics of lateral EC neural signals were more stable than during free foraging (Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2018

claim: The dynamics of lateral EC neural signals were more stable during structured tasks than during free foraging.
source: During a structured task in which the animal ran repeated laps on a maze separated into different trials, neural trajectories through population activity space were similar across trials, illustrating that the dynamics of lateral EC neural signals were more stable than during free foraging (Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2018

claim: Temporal coding was improved for time within a trial during the structured task compared to episodes of free foraging.
source: Consistently, temporal coding was improved for time within a trial during the structured task compared to episodes of free foraging.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2018

claim: Temporal information in the lateral EC might inherently arise from the encoding of experience.
source: These findings support the notion that temporal information in the lateral EC might inherently arise from the encoding of experience (Tsao et al., 2018).

claim: Slowly drifting activity patterns have been observed in the human medial temporal lobe.
source: Slowly drifting activity patterns have been observed also in the human medial temporal lobe (Folkerts et al., 2018) and EC specifically (Lositsky et al., 2016).

claim: Slowly drifting activity patterns have been observed in the EC specifically.
source: Slowly drifting activity patterns have been observed also in the human medial temporal lobe (Folkerts et al., 2018) and EC specifically (Lositsky et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lositsky et al., 2016

claim: A representation of time within a known trajectory in the alEC could underlie the encoding of temporal relationships between events.
source: A representation of time within a known trajectory in the alEC could underlie the encoding of temporal relationships between events in our task, where participants repeatedly navigated along the route to learn the positions of objects.

claim: Temporal mapping in the alEC might help integrate hippocampal spatio-temporal event maps.
source: Hence, temporal mapping in the alEC as we report here might help integrate hippocampal spatio-temporal event maps (Deuker et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculative interpretation connecting findings to prior work

claim: The alEC activated more strongly for the third of trials in which participants recalled temporal information most accurately compared to the third of trials in which temporal precision was lowest.
source: The alEC activated more strongly for the third of trials in which participants recalled temporal information most accurately compared to the third of trials in which temporal precision was lowest (Montchal et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Montchal et al., 2019

claim: The alEC represents the temporal structure of events after learning.
source: Going beyond the relationship of univariate activation differences to the precision of temporal memory recall, we focused on the content of alEC activation patterns and demonstrate that the alEC represents the temporal structure of events after learning.

claim: If alEC neural populations traverse similar population state trajectories on each lap, they would carry information about time within a lap.
source: If alEC neural populations traverse similar population state trajectories on each lap, they would carry information about time within a lap.

claim: A given object would be associated with a similar alEC population state on each lap.
source: A given object would be associated with a similar alEC population state on each lap.

source: Associations with temporally drifting signals during the learning task would result in representational changes relative to the baseline scan that, if reactivated in the post-learning picture viewing task, reflect the experienced temporal structure of object encounters.

claim: This interpretation is in line with data from rodent electrophysiology.
source: While this interpretation is in line with data from rodent electrophysiology (Tsao et al., 2018) and the framework proposed by the temporal context model (Howard and Kahana, 2002; Howard et al., 2005) as well as evidence for neural contiguity effects in image recognition tasks (Howard et al., 2012; Folkerts et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to relevant literature

claim: This interpretation is in line with the framework proposed by the temporal context model.
source: While this interpretation is in line with data from rodent electrophysiology (Tsao et al., 2018) and the framework proposed by the temporal context model (Howard and Kahana, 2002; Howard et al., 2005) as well as evidence for neural contiguity effects in image recognition tasks (Howard et al., 2012; Folkerts et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical framework

claim: This interpretation is in line with evidence for neural contiguity effects in image recognition tasks.

claim: The study cannot test the reinstatement of specific activity patterns from the learning phase directly since fMRI data were only collected during the picture viewing tasks.
source: we cannot test the reinstatement of specific activity patterns from the learning phase directly since fMRI data were only collected during the picture viewing tasks in this study.

claim: During learning, an object might become associated with preceding and successive objects, with stronger associations for objects closer in the sequence.
source: During learning, an object might become associated with preceding and successive objects, with stronger associations for objects closer in the sequence (Metcalfe and Murdock, 1981; Lewandowsky and Murdock, 1989; Jensen and Lisman, 2005).

claim: The reactivation of associated objects during the post-learning picture viewing task could drive similarity increases for objects close together in the sequence.
source: In this framework, the reactivation of associated objects during the post-learning picture viewing task could drive similarity increases for objects close together in the sequence.

claim: Object representations in lateral occipital cortex (LOC) were stable between the picture viewing tasks.
source: Object representations in lateral occipital cortex (LOC) were stable between the picture viewing tasks.

claim: Previous studies have observed evidence for cortical reinstatement during memory retrieval.
source: Previous studies have observed evidence for cortical reinstatement during memory retrieval (Nyberg et al., 2000; Wheeler et al., 2000; Polyn et al., 2005), modulated by hippocampal-entorhinal activity (Bosch et al., 2014).

claim: Cortical reinstatement during memory retrieval is modulated by hippocampal-entorhinal activity.
source: Previous studies have observed evidence for cortical reinstatement during memory retrieval (Nyberg et al., 2000; Wheeler et al., 2000; Polyn et al., 2005), modulated by hippocampal-entorhinal activity (Bosch et al., 2014).

claim: The study did not observe classification accuracies exceeding chance levels for objects from nearby sequence positions in LOC.
source: We did not observe classification accuracies exceeding chance levels for objects from nearby sequence positions in LOC, which one would expect if associative retrieval of objects accompanied by cortical reinstatement were to underlie our effects.

claim: These results fail to provide evidence for the notion that the reactivation of object representations drove the effects.
source: Hence, these results fail to provide evidence for the notion that the reactivation of object representations drove our effects.

claim: The highly-controlled design of the study supports the interpretation that alEC representations change through learning to map the temporal event structure.
source: Importantly, the highly-controlled design of our study supports the interpretation that alEC representations change through learning to map the temporal event structure.

claim: The order of object presentations during the scanning sessions was randomized and thus did not reflect the order in which objects were encountered during the learning task.
source: The order of object presentations during the scanning sessions was randomized and thus did not reflect the order in which objects were encountered during the learning task.

claim: The assignment of objects to positions was randomized across participants.
source: Since the assignment of objects to positions was randomized across participants and we analyzed pattern similarity change from a baseline scan, our findings do not go back to prior associations between the objects, but reflect information learned over the course of the experiment.

claim: The findings do not go back to prior associations between the objects, but reflect information learned over the course of the experiment.
source: Since the assignment of objects to positions was randomized across participants and we analyzed pattern similarity change from a baseline scan, our findings do not go back to prior associations between the objects, but reflect information learned over the course of the experiment.

claim: The object images were presented during the scanning sessions not only in the same random order, but also with the same presentation times and inter-stimulus intervals.
source: Further, we presented the object images during the scanning sessions not only in the same random order, but also with the same presentation times and inter-stimulus intervals; thereby ruling out that the effects we observed relate to temporal autocorrelation of the BOLD-signal.

claim: The experimental design rules out that the effects observed relate to temporal autocorrelation of the BOLD-signal.
source: Further, we presented the object images during the scanning sessions not only in the same random order, but also with the same presentation times and inter-stimulus intervals; thereby ruling out that the effects we observed relate to temporal autocorrelation of the BOLD-signal.

claim: The long time scales of lateral EC temporal codes differ from the observation of time cells in the hippocampus and medial EC.
source: The long time scales of lateral EC temporal codes differ from the observation of time cells in the hippocampus and medial EC, which fire during temporal delays in highly trained tasks (Pastalkova et al., 2008; MacDonald et al., 2011; Eichenbaum, 2014; Kraus et al., 2015; Mau et al., 2018; Heys and Dombeck, 2018).

claim: Time cells fire during temporal delays in highly trained tasks.
source: The long time scales of lateral EC temporal codes differ from the observation of time cells in the hippocampus and medial EC, which fire during temporal delays in highly trained tasks (Pastalkova et al., 2008; MacDonald et al., 2011; Eichenbaum, 2014; Kraus et al., 2015; Mau et al., 2018; Heys and Dombeck, 2018).

claim: Time cell ensembles change over minutes and days.

claim: Time cell firing has been investigated predominantly in the context of short delays in the range of seconds.
source: Time cell ensembles change over minutes and days (Mau et al., 2018), but their firing has been investigated predominantly in the context of short delays in the range of seconds.

source: In our task, one lap of the route took approximately 4.5 min on average; comparable to the 250s-duration of a trial in Tsao et al. (2018).

source: In humans, local and global functional connectivity patterns suggest a preserved bipartite division of the EC, but along not only its medial-lateral, but also its anterior-posterior axis (Navarro Schröder et al., 2015; Maass et al., 2015).

claim: Via entorhinal subdivisions, cortical inputs from the anterior-temporal and posterior-medial memory systems might converge onto the hippocampus.

claim: Hexadirectional signals in pmEC during imagination are putatively related to grid-cell population activity.

source: One potential explanation for the absence of evidence for a spatial distance signal in pmEC might be the way in which we cued participants' memory during the picture viewing task.

source: Due to the periodic nature of grid-cell firing, different locations might not result in diverging patterns of grid-cell population activity.
